title: Systems Thinking: Foundations
description: Editable version of the complete Mayne Leadership Systems Thinking: Foundations course, including its original explanations, practice activities, application, and reflection prompts.
author: Joshua Mayne

blocks.title: Stop chasing events. See the system.

blocks.body: Systems thinking helps us understand how parts, relationships, patterns, feedback, delays, assumptions, and consequences interact to produce results over time.
An executive message arrives: “Unit performance has dropped 18%. The backlog is growing and employees are working more overtime. Productivity is the problem. We need people to work faster.”

−18%Performance
+26%Backlog
+31%Overtime
+19%Errors
↓Morale

blocks.body:
Good systems thinking begins with restraint.
Several explanations are plausible. The visible event does not yet tell us what structure is producing the behavior.
Start at the lowest level: parts, connections, purpose, and boundary.

blocks.title: Linear thinking looks for a cause. Systems thinking looks for a structure.

blocks.body:
A
→
B
vs.
A web of relationships changing over time
Linear thinking can be useful for simple problems. It becomes risky when causes interact, accumulate, feed back, or arrive after delays.
Core shift: Ask “What caused this?” when the problem is simple. Ask “What relationships are producing this behavior over time?” when the problem is systemic.

blocks.title: A system is more than a collection of things.

blocks.body: Select each card and move horizontally. All three must be explored.

items.title: PARTS
items.text: The people, resources, processes, information, rules, tools, and other elements that exist inside the system.

items.title: CONNECTIONS
items.text: The relationships among the parts. Connections determine how changes move through the system and how one part affects another.

items.title: PURPOSE
items.text: What the system actually produces or is organized to accomplish. A system can produce outcomes nobody explicitly intended.

blocks.title: What belongs inside the system you are studying?

blocks.body: Inputs move through processes, producing outputs and outcomes.
Explore all four. The distinctions matter because improving output does not always improve the outcome.

items.title: INPUT
items.text: What enters the system: demand, people, information, resources, policy, technology, and constraints.

items.title: PROCESS
items.text: What the system does with those inputs: routing, decisions, handoffs, approvals, work, and quality checks.

items.title: OUTPUT
items.text: What is produced immediately: cases completed, products delivered, reports finished, calls answered.

items.title: OUTCOME
items.text: The larger result or effect: quality, timeliness, readiness, trust, mission impact, or sustained performance.

blocks.title: Stocks and flows explain why “more output” can still leave a growing problem.

blocks.body: A stock is something that accumulates. In this case, backlog. It changes according to what flows in and what flows out.

blocks.title: Starting stock and flows
blocks.rows:
Variable | Value
Backlog | 100
Inflow (new work + rework) | 25
Outflow (completed work) | 18

blocks.title: Run the backlog calculation
blocks.body: Start with backlog 100. Add 10 incoming items, complete 10, then add 5 rework items. Record backlog after each change. Which changes increase demand?

items.title: Worked example
items.text: 100 + 10 = 110; 110 − 10 = 100; 100 + 5 = 105. Backlog can grow even while output improves when total inflow exceeds outflow.

blocks.title: Rework is demand the system creates for itself.

blocks.body: Flip all three cards.

items.back: Leaders usually notice incoming demand because it arrives as obvious new work.
Errors create work that re-enters the system looking like more demand.
If faster work lowers quality, hidden inflow can increase even while visible output rises.

lessons.title: Events, Patterns, Structures, and Mental Models

blocks.body: Events are visible. Patterns, structures, and mental models sit underneath.

items.title: EVENTS
items.text: What happened? Example: backlog increased 26%.

items.title: PATTERNS
items.text: What keeps happening? Example: errors rise after overtime spikes.

items.title: STRUCTURES
items.text: What relationships create the pattern? Example: coaching, quality checks, incentives, handoffs, staffing, and process design.

items.title: MENTAL MODELS
items.text: What assumptions help create or sustain the structure? Example: “Busy means productive.”

blocks.body: Classify each statement as an event, pattern, structure, or mental model.

items.title: Errors rise after each overtime surge
Supervisors lose coaching time when escalations rise
“Training is time away from real work”
Turnover rises months after morale falls

blocks.body: Polarity, feedback, delays, and indicators reveal how the system moves.

blocks.title: “+” and “−” describe direction—not good or bad.

blocks.body: If the first variable increases, what tends to happen to the second, all else equal?

blocks.title: Match each relationship to its polarity
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Same direction is +; opposite direction is −.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Polarity describes direction, not good or bad.

items.back: Amplifies change. Growth can create more growth; decline can create more decline.
Counteracts change. Pushes the system toward a target, limit, or equilibrium.

blocks.title: Cause and effect can be separated by time.

blocks.body: Advance through the hiring example. Interventions can look weak before their effects have had time to arrive.

blocks.title: Hiring takes time to produce capacity

items.title: Month 0
items.text: Hire approved — No new capacity yet.

items.title: Month 1
items.text: Training load ↑ — Experienced staff pulled from work.

items.title: Month 2
items.text: Capacity dips — Intervention can look weak.

items.title: Month 4
items.text: Proficiency ↑ — New staff become more independent.

items.title: Month 6
items.text: Backlog responds — Capacity finally increases.

items.title: Lesson
items.text: Do not overcorrect — Define expected delay and monitor leading indicators.

blocks.title: WHY FIXES CAN MAKE THINGS WORSE

blocks.body: Recurring structures create familiar traps—and reveal leverage.
Select all three cards.

items.title: Fixes That Fail
items.text: A quick fix relieves a symptom but creates delayed consequences that recreate or worsen the problem.

items.title: Shifting the Burden
items.text: A symptomatic solution reduces pressure to invest in the deeper capability or structural fix.

items.title: Limits to Growth
items.text: Initial success slows or reverses because a limiting constraint becomes dominant.

blocks.title: Short-term relief can create delayed harm.

items.title: Backlog

items.title: Relief
items.text: Consider how this change affects the next step in the sequence.

blocks.body: Delayed consequence: fatigue → errors → rework → backlog. The fix is attractive because relief arrives before the harm.

blocks.title: Symptom relief can reduce pressure to build the deeper capability.

blocks.body: Overtime / quotas
Fast relief, but dependence grows.
Capability + process improvement
Slower relief, but structural improvement.
Warning sign: the more the organization relies on the quick-relief path, the less urgency it feels to strengthen the fundamental solution.

blocks.title: Success can expose the constraint that eventually slows success.

blocks.body: Better tools or staffing increase throughput.
Supervisor capacity, approvals, training load, or quality review becomes dominant.
Leverage question: What constraint must be relieved for improvement to continue?
Flip all four cards and look for the behavior each belief may produce.

items.back: May reward visible activity over actual outcomes.

items.front: “Training is time away from real work.”
items.back: May underinvest in future capability and increase dependence on experienced staff.
May hide process, workload, incentive, and quality-system causes.

items.front: “If output is low, raise the quota.”
items.back: May increase pace while creating fatigue, errors, and rework.

blocks.title: Choose interventions that change the structure—not just the pressure.

blocks.body: Select the two interventions you believe have the highest structural leverage.

blocks.title: Choose two interventions with structural leverage
blocks.body:
Choose two interventions, explain their leverage, and identify any tradeoff.

  • Remove duplicate approvals — Structural
  • Protect coaching time — Capability
  • Move quality checks earlier — Prevention
  • Hire additional staff — Capacity
  • Increase overtime — Symptom relief
  • Raise production quotas — Pressure
